events.blurb: The Supreme Court invalidates provisions of Coahuila’s penal code criminalizing voluntary abortion and establishes constitutional reasoning against absolute criminalization. This specific judgment is not an identical statutory reform in every Mexican state or proof of uniform service access.

events.title: Dobbs overturns Roe and Casey’s US abortion protection
events.blurb: In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Supreme Court overturns Roe and Casey and holds that the federal Constitution does not confer a right to abortion. The ruling permits divergent state restrictions and protections; it does not itself enact one nationwide abortion ban.

events.title: France constitutionally guarantees freedom to have an abortion
events.blurb: Parliament approves a constitutional amendment in March 2024 guaranteeing freedom to have recourse to abortion under conditions determined by law. The amendment is promulgated on 8 March. This strengthens constitutional protection without making access unconditional.

events.title: Russian women win voting rights before the Bolshevik takeover
events.blurb: Campaigning by women’s organizations helps secure voting rights under the Provisional Government in 1917. Women participate in elections that year, including for the Constituent Assembly. This milestone precedes the Bolshevik seizure of power and is not a claim that political equality is complete.

events.title: China’s Marriage Law recognizes free choice and easier divorce
events.blurb: The 1950 Marriage Law recognizes free choice in marriage and expands access to divorce. It is a major reform of family relations under the new People’s Republic. Enactment and its uneven implementation are different matters; it does not establish complete equality in everyday life.

events.title: Tunisia broadens legal access to abortion
events.blurb: Tunisia’s 1973 reform broadens the grounds for legal abortion after a more limited 1965 change. It permits abortion during the first three months under a medical framework, with specified grounds later. The milestone concerns the historical law, not a guarantee of equal practical access.

events.title: The US Comstock Act restricts mailing abortion and contraceptive materials
events.blurb: Congress enacts the Comstock Act on March 3, restricting the mailing of articles intended for abortion or contraception and associated information. The entry describes the 1873 statute; later amendments and court interpretations change its reach.
events.reason: The Office of Legal Counsel’s historical account, pages 3–4 and footnote 6, identifies the March 3, 1873 act and its original mailing provisions. No claim about present enforceability is made.

events.title: Colorado expands the circumstances permitting abortion
events.blurb: Colorado reforms its abortion law to permit abortions in specified circumstances, including pregnancies likely to cause the pregnant woman’s death and cases of rape or incest. This is a limited reform before Roe, rather than unrestricted legalization.
events.reason: The nonpartisan Colorado Legislative Council’s 2024 Amendment 79 Blue Book analysis dates the limited reform to 1967 and lists these circumstances. The marker represents the state capital.

events.title: Hawaii reforms abortion law before Roe
events.blurb: Hawaii’s Act 1 repeals earlier abortion provisions and permits termination of a nonviable pregnancy under specified conditions. The 1970 act requires a licensed physician, a qualifying hospital and state domicile or at least ninety days’ physical presence. These are historical conditions, not a description of later Hawaii law.
events.reason: The enacted Act 1 appears on pages 1–2 of the 1970 Hawaii session laws; its residency, hospital and nonviability conditions prevent an unqualified legalization claim.

events.title: New York legalizes abortion before Roe
events.blurb: New York legalizes abortion in 1970, three years before Roe v. Wade. The reform is a state-law milestone; it does not establish a nationwide right or imply that earlier restrictions and practical barriers immediately disappear everywhere.
events.reason: The New York State Legislative Women’s Caucus history, page 36, identifies the 1970 law, its sponsors and its passage; the point marks Albany rather than every affected provider.

events.title: Washington voters approve abortion reform in Referendum 20
events.blurb: On November 3, Washington voters approve Referendum 20. It permits abortion within four lunar months after conception, before quickening, subject to residency and consent requirements. The historical law includes husband-consent requirements for a married woman living with her husband and guardian consent for an unmarried minor under eighteen.
events.reason: The 1970 official voter pamphlet supplies the exact limited eligibility and consent terms. The legislature’s referendum history records approval on November 3, 1970; this does not describe present state law.

events.title: The Hyde Amendment restricts federal abortion funding
events.blurb: Congress first enacts the Hyde Amendment on September 30, restricting federal abortion funding through an appropriations provision and limiting Medicaid coverage. The original version has a life-saving exception. Later versions change the exceptions; this funding restriction is distinct from a nationwide criminal ban on abortion.
events.reason: Harris v. McRae recounts the initial September 30, 1976 enactment and varying annual exceptions, including the original life-saving exception (448 U.S. 302–304).

events.title: Harris v. McRae upholds the Hyde funding restriction
events.blurb: On June 30, the US Supreme Court upholds the challenged Hyde Amendment restrictions. It holds that Medicaid does not require a participating state to fund medically necessary abortions for which federal reimbursement is unavailable under Hyde. The decision concerns public funding, rather than a general prohibition on obtaining an abortion.
events.reason: The original Supreme Court opinion gives the June 30, 1980 date and distinguishes the Title XIX funding obligation and constitutional challenge. The description does not assert that state-funded coverage is forbidden.

events.title: Casey preserves abortion protection but changes the legal test
events.blurb: On June 29, the Supreme Court reaffirms Roe’s central protection before viability while replacing its trimester framework with an undue-burden standard for abortion restrictions. It invalidates Pennsylvania’s spousal-notification requirement while sustaining other challenged provisions. Dobbs overturns Roe and Casey in 2022.
events.reason: The original 1992 opinion supplies the ruling date, viability protection, undue-burden test and different treatment of the challenged Pennsylvania provisions. Dobbs supplies the subsequent reversal.

events.title: The FACE Act protects access to reproductive-health facilities
events.blurb: Congress enacts the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act. It prohibits force, threats and physical obstruction interfering with people obtaining or providing reproductive-health services, including abortion, and intentional damage to facilities. Its protections also cover pregnancy counseling facilities and places of religious worship; it does not itself legalize abortion nationwide.
events.reason: The DOJ’s archived reproductive-rights explanation dates enactment to 1994; its statutes-enforced explanation specifies the protected services, facilities and places of worship.

events.title: The FDA first approves mifepristone for medication abortion
events.blurb: In September, the Food and Drug Administration first approves Mifeprex, containing mifepristone, for medication abortion through seven weeks of pregnancy. This is a federal drug-approval milestone. Later labeling and access rules change; FDA approval does not itself guarantee access under every state’s laws.
events.reason: The FDA’s own question-and-answer page dates first approval to September 2000 and distinguishes the original seven-week indication from the 2016 extension. No current availability or treatment instructions are asserted.

events.title: New York enacts the Reproductive Health Act
events.blurb: On January 22, New York enacts the Reproductive Health Act. It authorizes abortion within twenty-four weeks, or when the fetus is not viable or an abortion is necessary to protect the patient’s life or health, according to the practitioner’s professional judgment. The statute strengthens state-law protection before Dobbs.
events.reason: The official S240 record records signing on January 22, 2019 and includes the enacted section 2599-bb eligibility language. This is the 2019 law, not a promise of current practical access.

events.title: Texas SB 8 restricts abortion through private civil enforcement
events.blurb: Effective September 1, Texas SB 8 prohibits most abortions after detection of embryonic or fetal cardiac activity and authorizes private civil actions against providers and people who knowingly aid prohibited abortions. A medical-emergency exception is included. This 2021 law takes effect before Dobbs; it is distinct from Texas’s later trigger prohibition.
events.reason: The Texas Legislature’s enrolled-bill summary gives the September 1, 2021 effective date, cardiac-activity restriction, medical-emergency exception and exclusive private civil enforcement. The summary does not impose a fixed week count.

events.title: Texas’s trigger abortion prohibition takes effect
events.blurb: On August 25, Texas’s Human Life Protection Act takes effect after the Supreme Court’s Dobbs judgment triggers the law. It prohibits abortion with a limited exception for a life-threatening physical condition. The statute was enacted in 2021; this marker records its 2022 commencement rather than its passage.
events.reason: The Texas State Law Library distinguishes enactment in 2021, the July 2022 Dobbs judgment and August 25 commencement. Chapter 170A supplies the qualified physical-condition exception.

events.title: California voters add reproductive freedom to the state constitution
events.blurb: On November 8, California voters approve Proposition 1, adding an explicit state constitutional protection for reproductive freedom, including the choice of abortion and the choice to use or refuse contraception. The measure concerns California’s constitution following Dobbs, rather than a new federal constitutional right.
events.reason: The Secretary of State’s certified Statement of Vote records Proposition 1’s approval on November 8, 2022; the official voter guide supplies its constitutional text.

events.title: Kansas voters reject the Value Them Both amendment
events.blurb: On August 2, Kansas voters reject a proposed amendment declaring that the state constitution does not secure a right to abortion or require abortion funding. Rejection leaves the constitution unchanged; it does not repeal every existing abortion regulation or establish unlimited access.
events.reason: The Kansas State Archives dates the rejection to August 2, 2022 and describes the proposal. The official ballot explains that a no vote makes no constitutional change.

events.title: Michigan voters approve the reproductive-freedom amendment
events.blurb: On November 8, Michigan voters approve Proposal 3, adding a right to reproductive freedom, including abortion and contraception, to the state constitution. The amendment takes effect on December 24. It allows regulation of abortion after fetal viability, subject to a life-or-health exception.
events.reason: The governor’s December 2022 implementation announcement distinguishes approval from December 24 commencement; the House Fiscal Agency’s proposal analysis reproduces the viability and life-or-health conditions.

events.title: Ohio adds a constitutional right to reproductive decisions
events.blurb: Ohio’s November Issue 1 amendment establishes a right to make and carry out reproductive decisions, including abortion, contraception and miscarriage care. Effective December 7, it permits abortion restrictions after fetal viability but protects abortion necessary for the pregnant patient’s life or health in the treating physician’s professional judgment.
events.reason: Ohio Constitution Article I section 22 supplies the right, viability exception and December 7, 2023 effective date. The November election is distinct from the August 2023 Issue 1.

events.title: Arizona voters approve a constitutional abortion right
events.blurb: Arizona voters approve Proposition 139 in the November 5 election. The amendment protects abortion before fetal viability and afterward when necessary to protect the pregnant individual’s life or physical or mental health in a treating health professional’s good-faith judgment. The governor proclaims the approved amendment law on November 25.
events.reason: The official proclamation verifies voter approval and November 25, 2024 proclamation. The Secretary of State’s final ballot-language explanation supplies the viability and life-or-health scope.

events.title: Florida’s six-week abortion restriction takes effect
events.blurb: On May 1, Florida’s Heartbeat Protection Act takes effect, replacing the previous fifteen-week limit with a prohibition after six weeks, subject to statutory exceptions. The state health agency’s notice links commencement to an April 1 Florida Supreme Court decision. This records implementation in 2024, following enactment in 2023.
events.reason: The Agency for Health Care Administration’s May 2024 emergency-rule notice explicitly records the May 1 start, six-week restriction, prior fifteen-week rule and statutory trigger; the 2024 statute provides the exceptions.

events.title: Florida’s abortion-rights amendment falls short of the approval threshold
events.blurb: On November 5, Amendment 4 receives about 57.17 percent of votes cast, below Florida’s sixty-percent requirement for constitutional amendments, and is not adopted. The proposal would have protected abortion before viability or when necessary for the patient’s health. A simple majority therefore does not change the state constitution.
events.reason: The official statewide results record 6,070,758 yes and 4,548,379 no votes. Florida Constitution Article XI section 5(e) requires sixty percent; the original proposal concerned previability and health protections. Approval is not inferred from a simple majority.

events.title: Colorado voters adopt a constitutional right to abortion
events.blurb: On November 5, Colorado voters approve Amendment 79, recognizing a state constitutional right to abortion and prohibiting state and local governments from denying or impeding it. The measure also removes the state constitutional restriction on public abortion funding; it does not remove separate federal funding restrictions.
events.reason: The Secretary of State’s historical election database gives the ballot question and statewide approval totals. The Legislative Council’s Blue Book distinguishes removal of the state funding ban from federal restrictions.

events.title: Missouri voters approve a reproductive-freedom amendment
events.blurb: On November 5, Missouri voters approve Amendment 3, adding a right to reproductive freedom, including abortion, to the state constitution. Its text allows restrictions after fetal viability with a life-or-health exception. This marks the 2024 constitutional vote; it does not assert that every clinic reopened immediately or describe later litigation and ballot measures.
events.reason: The Secretary of State’s official results record Amendment 3’s approval; the 2024 ballot-measures page supplies its scope. The description explicitly separates the vote from implementation and later developments.

events.title: Leaving Russia after the invasion: anti-war exile and flight from mobilization
events.blurb: After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, some people leave Russia because they oppose the war and do not want to support it; others fear repression for dissent or being sent to fight. These motives can overlap. A second major departure wave follows the September 21 mobilization announcement. Human Rights Watch documents both waves and the crackdown on anti-war speech; Reuters interviews describe opposition to the invasion and fear of the call-up. Georgia and Kazakhstan are among the destinations. Not everyone who leaves has the same political views or refugee status. The 2022–2023 interval highlights the initial waves and early aftermath, not the end of exile. Arrows are schematic connections from Russia to representative destinations, not individual journeys or migration counts.
events.reason: Human Rights Watch documents the two 2022 departure waves and repression of anti-war dissent. Reuters reporting of September 27, 2022 includes interviews with Russians leaving for Georgia who oppose the invasion and fear mobilization, and reports departures toward Kazakhstan. The bounded 2022–2023 viewing interval covers those waves and their early aftermath, not the end of exile. Representative Moscow-to-Tbilisi and Moscow-to-Almaty links are schematic, not claims about individual itineraries or departure volumes.
